content: Otitis externa is an inflammatory condition affecting the external auditory canal. The primary bacterial pathogens responsible for this condition are Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus. Fungal infections, such as those caused by Candida albicans and Aspergillus niger, can also lead to otitis externa, particularly in cases of otomycosis. Additionally, inflammatory dermatoses, including eczema, seborrhea, and psoriasis, may spread to the ear canal and contribute to the condition. The external auditory canal becomes vulnerable to infection when its epithelial integrity is compromised. This can occur due to sudden changes in humidity, which degrade the epithelial barrier, reduce cerumen production, and increase the pH of the ear canal, creating an environment conducive to bacterial or fungal growth. The gross pathological findings in otitis externa include erythema of the ear canal, scaling and shedding of the skin resembling eczema, visible swelling of the ear canal, and, in some cases, cellulitis of the pinna or otorrhea. Otitis externa is categorized into acute, chronic, or malignant forms based on the duration, severity, and extent of the infection. It is essential to differentiate otitis externa from other conditions that present with similar symptoms, such as otitis media, infectious myringitis, sinusitis, and Meniere's disease. Acute otitis externa is relatively common, with an annual incidence of approximately 801 cases per 100,000 individuals in the United States and 140 cases per 100,000 individuals in the Netherlands. Malignant necrotizing otitis externa, a severe form of the disease, has a case fatality rate of 10-20%. Acute otitis externa predominantly affects adults aged 65-74 years, while malignant otitis externa is more common in individuals over 50 years old, particularly those with diabetes mellitus or other conditions causing immunosuppression. Malignant necrotizing otitis externa is associated with immunocompromised states, including diabetes mellitus and chemotherapy. The primary symptoms of otitis externa include pain, itching, and swelling of the ear canal. Malignant necrotizing otitis externa may present with more severe symptoms, such as intense ear pain, facial paralysis, difficulty opening the mouth, and dysphagia. Laboratory findings typically reveal evidence of bacterial or fungal infection, and imaging studies, particularly CT scans, are crucial for diagnosing malignant necrotizing otitis externa. CT imaging can delineate the extent of infection, including its spread to the temporal and intracranial bones, and identify associated complications such as cranial nerve involvement. Scintigraphic imaging with Technetium-99m or Gallium Citrate Ga-67 can further aid in assessing the extent of infection and inflammation. Treatment of acute otitis externa involves cleaning the external auditory canal and administering topical antimicrobial therapy. Systemic antibiotics are reserved for cases with infection extending beyond the ear canal or in patients with specific risk factors. Analgesics, such as acetaminophen or NSAIDs, may be used to manage pain, either alone or in combination with opioids. The prognosis of otitis externa depends on the presence of complications. Acute otitis externa typically resolves without treatment within a few days, while chronic cases may persist without appropriate intervention. Malignant necrotizing otitis externa has a poor prognosis if left untreated, with potential complications including cranial nerve palsies, osteitis of the skull base, and osteomyelitis of the temporal bone. However, with timely and appropriate treatment, the prognosis for acute and chronic otitis externa is generally favorable.
